archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran bridge starter)
archetype.definition: A big, sturdy 11-year veteran who wins by taking short and intermediate answers on time and protecting the ball from sacks and fumbles, but who lacks the deep accuracy and late-down playmaking to lift an offense on his own.

report.headline: Volume masks a below-average passer who fades when the game is close
report.take:
Brissett is what his career says he is: a capable fill-in whose best years, 2019 and 2022, graded around the top third by EPA per play, and whose other seasons sat in the bottom half. This season fits the second group. His 5.82 yards per attempt ranks 44th of 54, and his -0.044 EPA per dropback ranks 31st. The 228.8 passing yards a game, 17th, come from throwing 39.3 times a game, not from efficiency. Now the context has flipped. He is listed as Baltimore's QB1, with Lamar Jackson on injured reserve after thumb surgery and expected out 6-to-10 weeks per head coach Jesse Minter. Most of the numbers below were built throwing to Trey McBride, Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne, not to anyone he will see in Baltimore.

The shape of the passing game is clear. Most of his charted throws travel under 10 air yards, and the very shortest ones hurt: throws behind the line cost -14.8 EPA in total. The real value is the intermediate window, 10 to 19 yards, worth +0.302 EPA per play with a 3.6 CPOE. Throws over the middle, at +0.171, are his best direction. He has pushed the ball more this year: aggressiveness is up to 22.6% from 16.5%, and his bad-throw rate fell to 12.1% from 16.7%. But the deep shots have not paid. On 20+ air yards he completes 22.2% with no touchdowns and three interceptions.

The totals hide where the EPA comes from. When trailing by 9 or more he has added +25.6 EPA with a 4.8 CPOE, which is soft-coverage, catch-up football. Within one score he has cost -46.1 EPA and thrown seven of his eight interceptions. On third down he has cost -35.6, converting 30.4% with no touchdowns and five picks. In close fourth quarters he is at -0.489 per play. All ten of his touchdown passes came in the red zone, yet his red-zone CPOE is -11.2. The scoring there came from volume of trips, not precision. McBride (+17.3 EPA on 80 targets) carried the passing game, while his second-most targeted receiver, Wilson, was a net negative on 74 targets.

The direction is down. Over his last three games he is at -0.117 EPA per dropback with a -4.9 CPOE and one touchdown on 120 attempts. Week 8 was his low point: pressured on 58.6% of dropbacks, only 58% of snaps, then a missed Week 9 practice. Baltimore gives him an offense that runs a bit more than average, plus a line that allows hits at the 24th-highest rate. Expect a lower-volume caretaker role whose fantasy floor comes from attempts and whose ceiling is capped by the deep ball and the money downs.

strengths.title: Intermediate timing throws over the middle
strengths.body: His best football is the 10-to-19-yard window, where he is completing 58.3% with positive CPOE and +21.7 total EPA. That is the only depth band paying for the rest of his game. Middle-of-field throws grade best by direction too, which fits a big pocket passer who reads it out and hits the in-cut or seam. This is a skill, not a fluke, so it should travel. What it needs in a new offense is a tight end or big slot who wins in that window, the way McBride did.

strengths.title: Avoids sacks and fumbles
strengths.body: His 5.6% sack rate ranks 15th, well under the 7.9% league average among qualifiers, and his pressure-to-sack rate ranks 11th. He has lost zero fumbles. His bad-throw rate of 12.1%, 7th-best, is a clear improvement on last year's 16.7%. It reflects quicker processing: time to throw is down 0.18 seconds from last year. That keeps drives alive even when the efficiency is poor, and it is the trait that makes him a viable bridge starter.

strengths.title: Sneak-and-push conversions
strengths.body: His legs are not a yardage source: 2.87 yards per carry overall and 1.63 on designed runs. They are a conversion tool, though. Designed runs succeed 78.9% of the time and his rushing EPA per carry is +0.329, the profile of a 235-pounder converting short yardage and goal-line sneaks. That role is stable, but it adds little fantasy value beyond the occasional touchdown.

concerns.title: Disappears when the game is close
concerns.body: Nearly all his positive value comes when trailing big. Within one score he has cost -46.1 EPA, and in close fourth quarters he is at -0.489 per play. Third down is worse still: -35.6 EPA total, a 30.4% conversion rate, five interceptions and no touchdowns, with an average of 7.4 yards to go. His career efficiency has been middling for years, so this is less noise than a limit. Expect it to show up again whenever the game stays tight.

concerns.title: The deep ball isn't there
concerns.body: On 36 throws of 20+ air yards he has completed 22.2% with a -15.3 CPOE, no touchdowns and three interceptions. The higher aggressiveness this year has not produced explosives. His career aDOT has always sat around 7 to 9, so stretching the field was never his game. With no vertical threat, defenses can squeeze the short and intermediate windows he relies on.

concerns.title: Recent slide, health and a new cast
concerns.body: His last three games show the worst efficiency of his season: -0.117 EPA per dropback, a -4.9 CPOE and a 7.0% sack rate. Week 8 included 58.6% pressure and a partial workload, and he did not practice in Week 9. He now has to learn a new receiving corps behind a Baltimore line that ranks 24th in hits allowed. Some of the slide may be circumstance, but none of it points to a rebound soon.

trend.note: He opened with two positive-EPA games in his first three, then turned volatile: a three-interception loss to the Giants and a -11.2 EPA dud in Dallas under heavy pressure. His most recent outing was 340 yards with no touchdowns. Efficiency over the last three games sits well below his season rate.

nextGame.headline: Carolina's missing pass rush should give him time to work
nextGame.body:
Carolina sets up well for a short-to-intermediate passer whose worst games came under pressure. The Panthers rank 32nd in both quarterback hit rate and sack rate, and 23rd in pass EPA allowed. That should give him a cleaner pocket than he saw in Dallas, and time to work the middle of the field. The catch is that Carolina ranks 2nd in limiting explosive passes. Without a deep game, he is more likely to be held to a long, efficient-but-capped day than a big one. The Panthers allow 236.9 quarterback yards a game, 8th-fewest. The tight end is where they leak: TE1s score 2.2 PPR points over their average against them (27th) at 0.40 EPA per target (26th). That suits his history of leaning on the tight end. WR1s, by contrast, have been held in check.

Availability tilts his way on the other side. Carolina is without LB Bobby Okereke (89% of snaps), which weakens coverage over the middle, and both CB Will Lee III and CB Mike Jackson are out. On his side, left guard-level starter Olaivavega Ioane (91% of snaps) left Monday's game questionable with a shoulder injury, and OT Emery Jones Jr. was a coach's-decision inactive. Interior protection is the piece to monitor. The Book has Carolina -2.5 with a 43.5 total, a modest-scoring, one-score game script, which is exactly where he has struggled most.

keyMatchups.title: No pass rush meets pressure-sensitive passer
keyMatchups.body: Carolina generates almost no hits or sacks, both ranking last in the league. His bad games correlate with pressure, so a clean pocket should keep his completion rate and decision-making near his early-season level. If Ioane can't go, Baltimore's interior is the one place that edge could erode.

keyMatchups.title: Middle of field vs. thinned coverage
keyMatchups.body: His intermediate and middle throws are his best, and Carolina is missing its top linebacker and two corners who played most snaps. Tight ends have found room against them all year. If Baltimore schemes the TE into the seams, he can stack completions.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive passes won't come easily
keyMatchups.body: Carolina ranks 2nd in explosive pass rate allowed, and his deep completion rate is 22.2%. Yards will have to come in chunks of 8 to 15, which raises the stakes on third down, where he converts 30.4%.

nextGame.watch: His third-down execution with a brand-new set of receivers: if Baltimore keeps him ahead of the sticks against this soft pass rush, he can manage the game; if not, his close-game problems resurface.

restOfSeason.body:
Lamar Jackson's estimated return date sits in late December, so Brissett looks like Baltimore's starter for most of the remaining stretch, health permitting. Expect fewer attempts than the 39.3 a game he averaged, because Baltimore passes slightly less than expected, and expect his volume-driven yardage to drop with them. I'd project roughly 190 to 245 passing yards and 0.8 to 1.5 touchdown passes a game. The sack avoidance and fumble security are real and should travel. The intermediate accuracy should travel too if a tight end or big slot wins inside.

What won't carry over is the catch-up production: much of his positive EPA came when trailing by two scores. In a more balanced offense that leans on the run and plays close games, the -0.218 EPA per play he posts within one score is the more honest baseline. The interception rate is roughly league-average and likely holds at 0.6 to 1.0 a game. Rushing stays a sneak-and-short-yardage tool worth single digits most weeks.
swingFactors: How quickly he builds timing with Baltimore's tight end and receivers
Interior line health (Ioane) and pressure rates

confidence.note: New team and receivers, recent health questions, and a season built in a different offense.
